title: The Salary Negotiation Trap Costing $30,000
hook: Never say this in a salary negotiation.

scenes.caption: In corporate hiring, saying this one sentence in your final interview can quietly cost you $30,000 over three years.
scenes.caption_roman: In corporate hiring, saying this one sentence in your final interview can quietly cost you $30,000 over three years.

scenes.caption: When a recruiter asks: 'What is your current compensation?', answering directly surrenders your entire psychological leverage.
scenes.caption_roman: When a recruiter asks: 'What is your current compensation?', answering directly surrenders your entire psychological leverage.

scenes.caption: Behavioral economists call this anchoring bias: the first number spoken sets the ceiling for all subsequent negotiation.
scenes.caption_roman: Behavioral economists call this anchoring bias: the first number spoken sets the ceiling for all subsequent negotiation.

scenes.caption: If you give a range like '$110k to $130k', the employer's brain automatically anchors to the lowest possible figure.
scenes.caption_roman: If you give a range like '$110k to $130k', the employer's brain automatically anchors to the lowest possible figure.

scenes.caption: The counter-script: 'I am focused on the value I will bring here. Based on market benchmarks for this role, what is your budgeted range?'
scenes.caption_roman: The counter-script: 'I am focused on the value I will bring here. Based on market benchmarks for this role, what is your budgeted range?'

scenes.caption: Force them to anchor first, then pause. The first person to speak after a salary offer almost always makes the concession. Follow Coercion Files for documented case files that protect your mind.
scenes.caption_roman: Force them to anchor first, then pause. The first person to speak after a salary offer almost always makes the concession. Follow Coercion Files for documented case files that protect your mind.
